title: VisDocAgentBench: Benchmarking Agents for Visually Rich Document Retrieval

visual_explainer.question: Where do visually rich document retrieval agents fail between target discovery, page examination, evidence-role integration, and final ranking?
visual_explainer.takeaway: A shared ranked-page contract separates static matching from iterative acquisition; bridge paths expose failures that direct one-shot matching hides.
visual_explainer.compared_with: Static single-vector and late-interaction visual/OCR rankers plus GPT-5.6-sol controls that remove iterative search, inspection, cropping, or route-specific text.

analysis.tldr: VisDocAgentBench evaluates static and agentic visual-document retrieval under the same top-10 ranked-page endpoint. Its strongest contribution is diagnostic: direct visual matching nearly saturates easy targets but collapses on hidden bridge paths; within the Qwen retrieval surface, iterative re-search and page inspection help, yet more input context and backend mismatch prevent a universal agent-policy claim.
analysis.problem: Most visual-document retrieval benchmarks measure one-shot query-page matching, while agentic benchmarks usually score downstream QA. Neither cleanly locates failures in iterative page acquisition, inspection, and ranked target discovery.
analysis.core_idea: Construct relation-preserving direct, one-bridge, and two-bridge queries over visually rich scientific documents, hide bridge concepts and document identifiers, and require every system to return ten opaque page IDs. Agents can search, inspect pages, use OCR/crops, and rank only discovered pages under a fixed step cap.
analysis.agent_loop: issue visual/OCR search → receive opaque page handles → inspect/OCR/crop candidates → reformulate search from observed evidence → integrate bridge roles → return ranked top-10 pages
analysis.retrieval_design: The benchmark contains 2,375 pages from 100 documents and 120 unique-target queries balanced across L1/L2/L3. Static systems and agents share the ranked-output contract. The main internal controls remove iterative search, page inspection, cropping, route-specific text, or supply annotated support pages.
analysis.evidence: Nemotron-ColEmbed reaches 97.5% R@1 on direct items but 2.5% on two-bridge items. For GPT-5.6-sol, removing iterative search lowers visual R@1 from 61.67 to 53.33 and OCR R@1 from 36.67 to 27.50; removing page inspection lowers them further. The visual route discovers 83.3% of gold targets versus 58.3% for OCR. However, the full visual agent uses 177K input tokens versus 101K for the fixed-candidate control.
analysis.why_it_matters: It strengthens the view that retrieval is an evidence-acquisition path—not just a score function. Representation determines discovery, inspection changes what becomes observable, and bridge-role integration determines whether discovered evidence is ranked correctly.
limitations: Agents use a Qwen single-vector frontend while the strongest static baseline uses Nemotron late interaction, so the broad static-versus-agent comparison is not backend matched.
The no-iterative control has independent batches and much less accumulated input context; policy and state delivery are not fully isolated.
Only six queries are cross-document, and the corpus is fixed English scientific pages, limiting generality.
Cropping/text ablations reverse by route or depth; no closed-model latency/dollar cost or offline OCR/index accounting is reported.
